item.title: US supreme court rules Trump can proceed with crackdown on mail-in voting
item.description:
President Trump can implement an executive order restricting mail-in ballots just months before the midterm elections, the Supreme Court said Monday . Why it matters: It's a win for the president, who has opposed mail-in voting for years, but the legal battle is far from over, and the exact impact on November's elections is still unclear. Driving the news: The Supreme Court said in the unsigned order that states lack standing to challenge the executive order because it was an "internal directive" that didn't harm the states that sued. "This internal directive does not regulate the States' voter registration processes," the court's order reads. "Nor does it impinge on the States' authority 'to create and enforce a legal code' for elections." item.title: Federal Judge Strikes Down Trump’s 75-Country Visa Ban
item.description:

Since January, people from those 75 countries—all located in Africa, Latin America, the Middle East, or Eastern Europe—have had their visa applications frozen or denied. On August 21, though, a federal judge in New York struck down this blanket visa ban, on the grounds that it violates the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965’s prohibition on nationality-based discrimination in issuing a visa. item.title: An ‘Economic D-Day’ That Must Overcome a Troubled History
item.description:
China hosted Iran’s deputy foreign minister for talks last week related to the US-Iran war, Beijing announced Sunday, disclosing the previously unreported meeting one day before Washington is expected to unveil “the toughest sanctions in history” against Tehran. The Trump administration has warned of an “ Economic D-Day ” for Iran and its trading partners, including China, a major importer of Iranian oil. Beijing has moved to insulate itself economically, slashing crude imports nearly 50% since the war started, according to The Wall Street Journal, and bolstering domestic energy. Experts warn that Beijing’s resilience could complicate Washington’s strategy. China, writes Shanghai Institutes for International Studies’ Zhao Long, is adept at “ containing spillover , reducing risks, diversifying dependencies, [and] avoiding strategic entanglement.” — Lauren Morganbesser

item.title: Tyler Cowen: The Least Bad Way to Regulate AI
item.description:
For how much longer will the fate of American artificial intelligence be steered from Silicon Valley rather than Washington? To watch the pace of AI progress, one might imagine that the answer to that question is rapidly shortening. Each milestone in the capability of AI increases the desire among lawmakers and much of the public to rein in the technology. That includes positive breakthroughs, such as the declaration last week by payments company Stripe that AI has achieved the long-awaited “singularity”: the ability to improve itself beyond what humans can contribute. It also includes worrying episodes, like the breach of the AI database Hugging Face last month by a powerful model gone rogue. Yet for all of the risks that AI brings, the harm caused by overregulating it would likely be much worse for the public. That is why AI developers and experts are devising proposals to promote AI…
